sources.title: 4.1 Demand and Supply at Work in Labor Markets
sources.author: Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald (OpenStax, Rice University)

verification.method: Opened 2026-11-13: title, authors, CC BY-NC-SA, and the no-LLM-training notice are present. Covers labor demand as derived from demand for the product, upward-sloping labor supply with a work-versus-leisure trade-off, equilibrium wage with surplus/shortage pressure, shifters of labor demand (demand for output, education/training and productivity, technology as substitute or complement, number of firms, regulation, other input prices) and labor supply (number of workers incl. population/immigration/aging, required education, government policies), technology and wage inequality, minimum wage and living wage as a price floor creating a labor surplus, and a debate over employment effects (typical estimates of reduced low-skill hiring, some contested studies finding no effect, no simple answer). The page does not discuss monopsony or employer market power.

sources.title: 14.1 The Theory of Labor Markets
sources.author: Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald (OpenStax, Rice University)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. OpenStax states that its content may not be used to train large language models without written permission. ECONOVA does not copy the text; it only links to and credits the source.

sources.author: Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald (OpenStax, Rice University)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. OpenStax states that its content may not be used to train large language models without written permission. ECONOVA does not copy the text; it only links to and credits the source.

verification.method: Opened 2026-11-13: title and book metadata present. Defines monopsony (one employer with market power, e.g. a single coal company in a town); the monopsonist hires where labor demand equals the marginal cost of labor, which exceeds the wage, so it hires fewer workers and pays less than a competitive market; lists setting minimum hourly wages among laws to balance power between workers and employers. The page does NOT analyze whether a minimum wage can raise employment under monopsony (that analysis in c05-l3 is a standard textbook extension written by the AI).
